title: HPDT Phys25/645P — Mr Lance Easton (Physiotherapists)
text:
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HPDT NO 1530/Phys25/645P
UNDER the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003
(the Act)
IN THE MATTER of a disciplinary charge laid against a health practitioner
under Part 4 of the Act
BETWEEN A PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT COMMITTEE appointed by
the PHYSIOTHERAPY BOARD OF NEW ZEALAND
Applicant

Introduction
[1] Mr Easton faces a single charge that he has acted in breach of his professional
obligations amounting to professional misconduct, as the complained of conduct is said to
amount to malpractice or negligence in relation to his scope of practice and has brought or
is likely to bring discredit to the profession.
The Charge
[2] There is, as has already been said a single charge; the particulars of which in summary
are:
• That on or about 29 December 2013, Mr Easton provided physiotherapy services
to [Mrs S] in a manner which was inappropriate and/or unprofessional in that he
had failed to obtain informed consent to the services to be provided; failed to
provide screening or other privacy measures; requested that she remove her
upper clothing; removed his shirt while providing services and hugged [Mrs S].
• On or about 8 October 2018, Mr Easton provided physiotherapy services to [Mrs
S] again in a manner which is said to be inappropriate and/or unprofessional in
particular: failed to obtain informed consent to the services provided; directed
and requested [Mrs S] to engage in a breathing exercise without obtaining her
consent and positioned himself inappropriately and/or in an unprofessional
manner while directing her to engage in such.
Law
[3] Mr Easton took no part in these proceedings; however, the following appear to be
beyond dispute:
• Mr Easton was registered as a physiotherapist on 2 March 2009.
• By 2013 (at least), Mr Easton was practising as a physiotherapist in the Thames
Coromandel area.
3

• It was while practising as a physiotherapist that on two occasions, Mr Easton
provided services to [Mrs S].
Onus and Standard of Proof
[4] The onus of proof is on the PCC to prove the charge to the requisite civil standard of the
balance of probabilities. The standard is applied flexibly and is dependent on the seriousness
of the matters to be proved and the consequences of proof.1
[5] The Tribunal is required to consider each particular independently and then
cumulatively, in the context of the overall charge. 2
Purpose of Disciplinary Proceedings
[6] When considering the charge it is submitted that the Tribunal should have regard to
the primary purpose of its disciplinary powers, which is the protection of the public and the
maintenance of professional standards.3 A further purpose is to maintain the integrity of the
profession. In Dentice v The Valuers Registration Board, Eichelbaum CJ described
professional disciplinary procedures as follows:4
Although, in respect of different professions, the nature of unprofessional or
incompetent conduct, which will attract disciplinary charges, is variously
described, there is a common thread of scope and purpose.
Such provisions exist to enforce a high standard of propriety and professional
conduct; to ensure that no person unfitted because of his or her conduct should be
allowed to practise the profession in question; to protect both the public, and the
profession itself, against persons unfit to practise; and to enable the profession or
calling, as a body, to ensure that the conduct of members conforms to the
standards generally expected of them …
1 Z v Dental Complaints Assessment Committee [2007] NZSC 45.
2 This principle is explained in Duncan v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee [1986] 1 NZLR 513 and
Chan v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee (Court of Appeal, CA 70/96, 7 August 1996).
3 Section 3 HPCA Act.
4 [1992] 1 NZLR 720.
4

[7] In B v Medical Council Elias J stated:5
The structure of the disciplinary processes set up by the Act, which rely in large part
upon judgment by a practitioner’s peers, emphasizes that the best guide to what
is acceptable professional conduct is the standards applied by competent,
ethical, and responsible practitioners. But the inclusion of lay representatives in
the disciplinary process and the right of appeal to this court indicates that usual
professional practice, while significant, may not always be determinative: the
reasonableness of the standards applied must ultimately be for the court to
determine, taking into account all the circumstances including not only practice
but also patient interests and community expectations, including the expectation
that professional standards are not to be permitted to lag. The disciplinary
process in part is one of setting standards. (Emphasis added)
Professional misconduct – two-step process
[8] It is well settled that there are two steps in assessing what constitutes professional
misconduct:6
…the test for whether a disciplinary finding is merited is a two-stage test based on
first, an objective assessment of whether the practitioner departed from
acceptable professional standards and secondly, whether the departure was
significant enough to attract sanction for the purposes of protecting the public.
Step One: Malpractice, negligence or discredit to the profession
[9] Section 100(1)(a) relates to professional misconduct that is malpractice or negligence.
As to malpractice, the Tribunal regularly refers to the dictionary definition, namely the
“immoral, illegal or unethical conduct or neglect of professional duties.”7 A finding of
negligence requires the Tribunal to determine:8
5 [2005] 3 NZLR 810.
6 H v Director of Proceedings [2018] NZHC 2175 at [19], citing McKenzie v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary
Tribunal [2004] NZAR 47 (HC) at [71].
7 See Cole v Professional Conduct Committee [2017] NZHC 1178 at [41].
8 Cole v Professional Conduct Committee [2017] NZHC 1178 at [42]. See also Nuttall Med/04/03P at [62].
5

Whether or not, in the Tribunal’s judgment, the practitioner’s acts or omissions fall
below the standards reasonably expected of a health practitioner in the
circumstances of the person appearing before the Tribunal.
[10] Section 100(1)(b) provides another route by which a practitioner may be found guilty of
professional misconduct. It is for the Tribunal to decide whether the conduct would be likely
to bring discredit to the profession. The leading statement with regard to bringing discredit
to the profession is found in Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand9
To discredit is to bring harm to the repute or reputation of the profession. The
standard must be an objective standard for the question to be asked by the Council
being whether reasonable members of the public, informed and with knowledge of
all the factual circumstances, could reasonably conclude that the reputation and
good standing of the nursing profession was lowered by the behaviour of the nurse
concerned.
[11] The High Court has also observed that:10
The legislature has entrusted the Tribunal, comprising in large part health
practitioners, with bringing their collective judgment to bear on individual fact
situations, and in determining whether or not conduct by a health practitioner is
likely to bring discredit on the medical profession. The decision in this regard
essentially calls for a value judgment. The Tribunal acts in a representative
capacity, formulating standards which of themselves are representative. It is an
expert body, well placed to assess and evaluate the seriousness of a practitioner’s
conduct.
Deference is appropriate in respect of the Tribunal’s judgment on such
matters.
9 [2001] NZAR 74 (HC) at [28].
10 Williams v Professional Conduct Committee [2018] NZHC 2472 at [103].
6

Step Two: Threshold
[12] The second step for establishing professional misconduct is for the Tribunal to consider
whether it is satisfied that the acts or omissions require a disciplinary sanction. The Tribunal
will impose a disciplinary sanction if it is satisfied that it is necessary in the particular
circumstances to protect the public and/or to maintain professional standards.11
[13] The leading authority on the issue of threshold is the High Court’s decision in Martin v
Director of Proceedings, where Courtney J found that “the threshold should not be regarded
as unduly high.”12 Martin has subsequently been approved and applied in a number of
decisions by the High Court.13 In particular, in PCC v R Justice Powell overturned the
Tribunal’s finding that the threshold had not been met, with reference to Martin, and
observed that:14
… It is after all a threshold rather than a substantive hurdle, and it is not
necessary to show that the respondent’s conduct was as serious as that of others
that have received penalties. I note in particular that in addition to protecting
the public and punishing the practitioner, a penalty can provide clarity to the
profession and assist the practitioner through the imposition of conditions on
practice. [Emphasis added]
[14] As to whether disciplinary sanction is warranted it has been noted that:
…ignorance of basic obligations that demonstrate incompetence, and the
potentially very significant consequences of the actions complained of, have
previously warranted disciplinary sanction;…15
Credibility
[15] The Tribunal is required to determine whether they consider the evidence of the
complainant to be credible.
11 See for example Ms E 347/Nur10/159P.
12 Martin v Director of Proceedings [2010] NZAR 333 (HC)at [32].
13 See for example Johns v Director of Proceedings [2017] NZHC 2843 at [85] and H v Director of Proceedings
[2018] NZHC 2175 at [25].
14 [2018] NZHC 2531 at [31].
15 Rodrigues (384/Ost11/173P).
7

[16] The leading authority for the test for credibility in this jurisdiction is the High Court’s
decision in Rabih v Professional Conduct Committee of the Dental Council in which it was held
that “no issue could be taken” with the principles outlined in Faryna v Chorny16 being applied
by the Tribunal:17
The real test of the truth of the story of a witness must be its harmony with the
preponderance of the probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily
recognise as reasonable in that place and in those conditions, with the following factors
being relevant:
a) The manner and demeanour of the witness when giving evidence.
b) Issues of potential bias, that is, to what extent was evidence given
from a position of self-interest.
c) Internal consistency or, in other words, whether the evidence of the
witness was consistent throughout, either during the hearing itself, or
with regard to previous statements.
d) External consistency or, in other words, was the evidence of the
witness consistent with that given by other witnesses.
e) Whether non-advantageous concessions were freely tendered.
[17] In applying the Faryna v Chorny framework used by Rabih the Tribunal should:
a. “… not place too much weight on demeanour, as “scientific research has
cast doubt on the possibility of being able to distinguish truth from
falsehood accurately, solely on the basis of appearances”;18 and
b. Not consider whether the evidence of a complainant or the practitioner is
biased or self-interested as “the evidence of a protagonist will inevitably be
vulnerable to a criticism on the ground of self-interest”; any consideration
16 Farynia v Chorny [1952] 2 DLR 354 (BCCA).
17 [2015] NZHC 1110, [2015] NZAR 1102 at [40 - 41]; as per the dictum stated by Canadian Appellate Court in
Faryna v Chorny
18 H v A Ltd [2014] NZEMPC 189 at [73(d)]; also see Martin v Director of Proceedings, at [7].
8

of bias is “more suitably deployed in the context of supporting witnesses
rather than the key participants themselves”.19
[18] The Tribunal has also previously commented, on the drawing of inferences, that:20
Inferences are logical conclusions from proven facts. It is well established that a
fact finding body such as the Tribunal can properly draw logical inferences,
providing it does so on the basis of facts which are proved to its satisfaction. It
cannot speculate or guess. (Emphasis added).
Relevant standards and guidelines
[19] The Physiotherapy Board’s standards of competence, including its Code of Ethics, are
highly relevant to the question of whether Mr Easton breached his professional obligations.
Codes of Ethics and other related statements cannot be expected to capture every instance
of behaviour that may reasonably be considered unacceptable or unprofessional. However,
the standards referred to below make it clear that physiotherapists have an obligation to
maintain, and avoid the blurring of, professional boundaries and to behave respectfully in
relation to patients.
[20] The charges arise from two appointments, one in 2013 and one in 2018. There were
different versions of the Code of Ethics and standards in force for each appointment. The
differences between the two Codes of Ethics are of form rather than substance, however, to
ensure clarity they have been outlined separately.
2011 Code of Ethics
[21] The principles set out in the Code of Ethics ‘Aotearoa New Zealand Physiotherapy Code
of Ethics and Professional Conduct 2011’ (2011 Code) “provide a set of guidelines for the
professional behaviour expected of all physiotherapists in Aotearoa New Zealand.”21 Where
the Code of Ethics uses the term ‘must’, it “sets a minimum standard that all physiotherapists
are obliged to achieve.”22
19 Rabih v Professional Conduct Committee at [58].
20 Gilgen Med07/60 & 07/61P at [34]-[35].
21 2011 Code of Ethics at pg. 1.
22 2011 Code of Ethics at pg. 5.
9

[22] Principle 1 of the Code of Ethics puts dignity and respect at the forefront, stating that
physiotherapists must:23
a. Respect the dignity, privacy, bodily integrity, and mental wellbeing of
patients/clients;24
b. behave in a respectful manner towards their patient/clients as well as their
whānau and family.25
[23] As to the physiotherapist patient relationship, the principle 2.10 provides that
physiotherapists must establish and maintain appropriate professional boundaries with
patients/clients and their whānau and families.
[24] The 2011 Code also dictates that physiotherapists must “act to promote the health and
wellbeing of the patient/client, while acknowledging and facilitating patient/client
autonomy”. This includes:
a. “clearly inform patients/clients of the purpose and nature of physiotherapy
interventions to enable all patients/clients to make an informed choice”
(principle 2.5);
b. “seek patient/client consent prior to providing physiotherapy services,
ensuring that patient/clients consent is freely given and appropriately
documented” (principle 2.6).
Other relevant standards – 2013
[25] The following relevant standards were in place in 2013:
a. Position Statement – Clear sexual boundaries in the patient –
physiotherapist relationship (December 2012) (the Position Statement).
The position statement provides, among other things, that:
23 2011 Code of Ethics at 1.1 and 1.2.
24 2011 Code of Ethics at 1.1.
25 2011 Code of Ethics at cl 1.2.
10

i. “The physiotherapist to patient relationship is not one of equality. In
seeking assistance, guidance and treatment the patient is
vulnerable.”26
ii. “The abuse of professional boundaries is not restricted to sexual
relationships but may include any conduct which crosses professional
boundaries, or may be reasonably construed by the patient as having
that purpose. Professional boundaries are defined as limits which
protect the space between the professionals power and the clients
vulnerability…”27
iii. “Sexual impropriety means any behaviour such as gestures or
expressions that are sexually demeaning to a patient, or which
demonstrate a lack of respect for the patients privacy, including but
not exclusively: inappropriate disrobing or inadequate draping
practices.”28
iv. “To avoid any misunderstanding or inappropriate conduct the
physiotherapist should employ the following safeguards:
•
Provide adequate information and explanation which helps to
avoid misunderstandings and misinterpretation.
• …
• Provide suitable facilities with screens for undressing, draping.
• ….
• Refrain from undue familiarity.
• …”
b. Physiotherapy New Zealand’s Standards of Practice from November 2012
(2012 Standards) are also relevant. The 2012 Standards provide that:
i. “The patient’s informed consent is obtained prior to commencing
assessment and again prior to commencing treatment and both are
26 Position Statement, cl 2.
27 Position Statement, cl 3.
28 Position Statement, cl 7.1.
11

documented in the patient record”29
ii. “Treatment options, including significant benefit, risks and side
effects, are discussed with the patient”30
iii. “The patient is given an opportunity to ask questions and discuss
treatment options”31
iv. “The physiotherapist checks with the patient to ensure that the
decision is accept or refuse treatment is given freely. The patient
may refuse treatment at any point without it prejudicing the
provision of care in the future”32
v. “The physiotherapist checks that the patient has understood the
information provided and documents this in the clinical records”33
vi. “The patients dignity and privacy are respected at all times”34
vii. “The physiotherapist establishes appropriate professional
boundaries with patients and their families”35
2018 Code of Ethics
[26] The Board issued a new Code of Ethics in May 2018 - Aotearoa New Zealand
Physiotherapy Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (2018 Code).
[27] Similarly to the 2011 Code, Principle 1 of the 2018 Code puts dignity and respect at the
forefront of practice. It states that physiotherapists must:36
a. respect the dignity, privacy, bodily integrity, and mental wellbeing of
patients.
29 2012 Standards, C1, pg. 13.
30 2012 Standards, C2, pg. 13.
31 2012 Standards, C3, pg. 13.
32 2012 Standards, C4, pg. 13.
33 2012 Standards, C5, pg. 13.
34 2012 Standards, B5, pg. 10.
35 2012 Standards, B7, pg. 11.
36 2018 Code of Ethics at 1.1 and 1.2.
12

b. conduct themselves in a respectful manner towards the patient as well as
their whānau, family and carers.
[28] As to the physiotherapist – patient relationship, the 2018 Code states that
physiotherapists must establish and maintain appropriate professional boundaries with
patients (principle 2.11). The commentary makes it clear that:37
Society trusts physiotherapists to act in the best interests of patients. A
power imbalance exists within the therapeutic relationship that can easily
lead to exploitation or abuse if that trust is not respected…
[29] With respect to informed consent, the 2018 Code provides:
2.5 clearly and adequately inform patients of the purpose and nature of the
physiotherapy intervention to enable all patients to make an informed choice.
Commentary: The patient is entitled to information about his or her diagnosis and
prognosis, care plan, alternative treatments, risks and benefits associated with
treatment, costs associated with treatment, results of any tests, and the name of
the physiotherapist providing care and any other relevant information. This
information must be provided in a form, language and manner that can be
understood by the patient. The patient must be given the time and opportunity to
ask questions and have them answered to their satisfaction. Where necessary and
practicable, an interpreter must be supplied. The physiotherapist should be
guided by the patient in ascertaining whether additional information is required to
enable the patient to make an informed choice and give informed consent.
2.6 seek patient consent prior to providing physiotherapy services, ensuring
that patient consent is freely given and appropriately documented.
Commentary: For most physiotherapy procedures verbal consent is usually
sufficient (however this should be documented in patient records). Written
consent is required in many cases including where there is significant risk of
adverse effects, a student is involved, experimental procedures, or when the
patient is involved in research. Written consent is not necessarily a safeguard for
the physiotherapist if the process of informed consent has not been fulfilled.
13

Getting patients to sign a non-specific consent to any future proposed treatment
is not acceptable. Consent must be obtained for every new treatment, or when
the patient’s circumstances change. Consent should be considered an ongoing
conversation between the physiotherapist and the patient and should be obtained
prior to each interaction. Physiotherapists should be alert to the possibility that a
patient may wish to withdraw consent to ongoing or future treatment and this
must be respected.
2018 – Standards
[30] The second charge relates to an appointment that occurred in October 2018, when the
Physiotherapy Standards Framework 2018 was in place. The framework contains the
following standards:
a. The Sexual and Emotional Boundaries Standard provides:
i. Maintaining clear professional boundaries is integral to the
physiotherapist-patient relationship.38
ii. Safeguarding professional boundaries involves (amongst other things):
A Ensuring appropriate informed consent is gained for all
examinations, treatment and asking the patient to disrobe.
B Ensuring appropriate patient draping.39
b. The Informed Consent Standard provides:
i. “1.1 Physiotherapists must seek patient informed consent before
providing any physiotherapy services, ensuring their consent is freely
given and appropriately documented”40
ii. “3.1 Physiotherapists must clearly and adequately inform the patient
of the purpose and nature of the physiotherapy intervention to enable
37 2018 Code of Ethics at 2.11.
38 Physiotherapy Standards framework 2018, pg. 76 at [2.1].
39 Physiotherapy Standards framework 2018, pg. 77 at [2.2].
40 Physiotherapy Standards framework 2018, pg. 50.
14

their informed choice”41
iii. “3.2 Patients have the right to sufficient information to make an
informed choice or give informed consent. This includes, but is not
limited to42
A an explanation of the patient’s condition
B an explanation of the options available, including an assessment
of the expected risks, side effects, benefits, and the costs, and
different treatment options including public and private where
appropriate
C The advice about treatment frequency, and estimated numbers
of treatments.”
Relevant cases
[31] Each case turns on its own facts and no two cases are alike. Nonetheless, aspects of
the following cases may be relevant and of some guidance to the Tribunal:
Providing physiotherapy services in a manner that was inappropriate and/or
unprofessional
[32] In McNair (680/Mrt14/289P), a medical radiation technologist was found to have
engaged in professional misconduct in relation to three patients, Ms H, Ms T and Ms N by
a. opening and closing Ms H’s gown around her hip area exposing her
underwear in circumstances where there was no prior warning given to Ms
H that this was necessary clinically and/or where this was inappropriate
professionally;
b. behaving in an inappropriate manner towards Ms T and/or conducted
himself inappropriately professionally by offering to deliver her x-rays to her
“over a drink”; and
c. placing both his hands on the sides of Ms N’s waist (one on each side)
without giving any prior warning that he intended to do so and in
41 Physiotherapy Standards framework 2018, pg. 51.
42 Physiotherapy Standards framework 2018, pg. 51 – 52.
15

circumstances where this physical contact was unwarranted clinically
and/or was inappropriate professionally.
[33] The Tribunal found that the conduct was malpractice and brought discredit to the
profession. The particular relating to Ms H’s gown only warranted disciplinary sanction
cumulatively; however, the particulars relating to Ms T and Ms N each warranted sanction
individually. In reaching this conclusion the Tribunal found at [71]:
A sanction is required in order to meet the primary objective of the Act;
namely to protect the public and maintain appropriate professional
standards for the medical radiation technologist profession. Mr McNair’s
conduct was a departure from acceptable professional standards. The
nature of a medical radiation technologist’s work is that they are
frequently alone with patients who are about to be or are in a state of
undress and who are therefore vulnerable. As a result, there is a
substantial onus on the practitioner to observe the highest standards of
professional conduct.
[34] Chum (1033/Phys18/420D), involved a charge that a physiotherapist inappropriately
touched and massaged a vulnerable patient during treatment for her vocal cords. The
Tribunal was asked to consider whether Mr Chum had unnecessarily asked the patient to
remove all of her clothes; failed to ask her to re-clothe herself; proceeded with the massage
despite the patient being naked; failed to adequately drape the patient during massage; and
asked to massage her clitoral region. The Tribunal concluded that separately each of these
sub-particulars was made out as malpractice, negligence or conduct bringing discredit to the
profession and warranted disciplinary sanction. The Tribunal also found that the massage
itself was not appropriate treatment for the patient’s clinical presentation and that this also
warranted disciplinary sanction.
[35] Sheela (1164/Nur20/491P), Mr Sheela, a registered nurse, was found to have
breached professional boundaries by, on two occasions giving a patient hug; kissing her on
two occasions; and on one occasion asking if he could get on the bed with her. The Tribunal
commented (at [139]):
16

As Ms S eloquently described, Mr Sheela overstepped the boundary on each
occasion by asking to hug her in circumstances where she was a patient, in
pain and alone at night with a male nurse.
[36] The Tribunal found that the patient was in a vulnerable position and the power
imbalance between a nurse and a patient was exacerbated because of her considerable pain.
The breach occurred in a setting where the patient was entitled to feel safe and be safe, and
the conduct interfered with her care.43
[37] Derry (143/Phys07/79D), Mr Derry, a physiotherapist, pulled the cups of a patient’s bra
down at the end of her appointment, exposing her breasts for a brief period, without any
clinical justification to do so. This was found to amount to malpractice and be conduct likely
to bring discredit to the profession. In reaching this conclusion the Tribunal stated “the
incident which occurred was very serious, and could in other circumstances have amounted to
an indecent assault” at [62]. The Tribunal also noted there was a power imbalance between
Mr Derry and the patient; the conduct was initiated by Mr Derry and he had total
responsibility for it; he failed to act in the best interests of the patient; and there was a
significant breach of trust (at [62]). While there was no evidence of sexual motivation, the
Tribunal found a “very serious error of judgment occurred” at [63]
Informed consent
[38] There are numerous cases that establish that failing to obtain informed consent
amounts to professional misconduct. The following cases provide some guidance:
a. In Lakra (714/Den15/309D), a dentist accepted that he had failed to inform
and advise the patient adequately as to treatment options and to obtain his
informed consent to the treatment which did take place. During a root
canal a part of the dentist’s instruments broke off in the root. He did not
inform the patient of this, and when the patient required further
treatments for infections still failed to tell the patient what had happened
43 At [141] - [146].
17

or advise alternative treatment options. The Tribunal found professional
misconduct was established and said (at [21]):
The serious nature of the Practitioner’s professional misconduct, and the
way that it engages the issues of the protection of the public and the
maintenance of professional standards, demands, in the Tribunal’s view,
the imposition of a penalty.
b. In Rodrigues (384/Ost11/173P), an osteopath was found to have failed to
obtain informed consent (among other things). He did not provide a
summary of techniques he was going to use in treatment or their purpose.
The Tribunal found (at [36]) that Mr Rodrigues’ evidence demonstrated a
“woeful understanding of the obligations of informed consent.”
c. In Krishnayya (Med06/46D), a surgeon was found to have failed to provide
adequate information before and after surgery, and therefore to obtain his
patient’s informed consent. The information provided to the patient about
the surgery and its risks was minimal as the surgeon had only a limited
understanding of the treatment. No information was given as to other
procedures or options.
d. In Harman v Director of Proceedings, the High Court upheld the Tribunal’s
finding of professional misconduct for failing to obtain a patient’s informed
consent prior to surgery. Dr Harman also failed to ensure adequate records
were maintained.
e. Finally, in Zimmerman (19/Den05/05D), a dentist did not obtain a patient’s
informed consent in that he failed to advise the patient of the risks of
inserting three unsplinted implants in her maxilla and his shortcomings
constituted a serious failure on his part.

[47] Mr Easton did not bring any equipment with him and directed her to lie on a bed. [Mrs
S] was extremely uncomfortable with this idea so told him that she preferred to be treated
on a chair and went and fetched a dining chair.
[48] A massage began but Mr Easton said to her that her shirt and bra were in the way and
asked her to remove her top. In an effort to maintain her modesty she went to the
bathroom, removed her top but not her bra and wrapped herself in a towel.
[49] After the massage, he told her she needed to undertake some breathing exercises
because she was tense and uptight. He then moved the chairs that they were sitting knee to
knee and got her to breathe with him.
[50] It was only after [Mrs S] became aware of reporting of other complaints about Mr
Easton that she made a complaint herself. She described it thus:
“When I saw this reporting, I felt angry at myself. I felt like if I had said something
earlier maybe some of those people would not have had to go through their
negative experiences.”
Credibility
[51] Whilst, Mr Easton has not participated in this process, we are nevertheless required to
form a view regarding the credibility of[Mrs S]. We find that [Mrs S] is credible, honest and
reliable.
Outcome
[52] We find that the charge and all particulars are proven and further, that Mr Easton’s
conduct is sufficiently serious to warrant a disciplinary sanction. The PCC submitted that Mr
Easton should have been aware of his responsibilities and that the onus was on him to
ensure patient privacy and dignity. Respect and dignity are fundamental to establishing a
trusting and functioning physiotherapist/patient relationship. That submission is accepted
by the Tribunal.
20

[53] We received helpful submissions from the PCC regarding similar cases. These are:
a. Chum (1033/Phys18/420D), involved a physiotherapist being found to
have engaged in professional misconduct by way of him inappropriately
touching and massaging a patient during treatment for her vocal cords. In
considering the appropriate penalty, the Tribunal was particularly
conscious of Mr Chum’s statement that he had not made a decision on
whether or not he wished to resume practice (and had not applied to
renew his practising certificate). In light of that, the Tribunal considered
that an order for suspension may be meaningless and a nugatory order of
no practical effect. However, the Tribunal commented that the remaining
orders (short of cancellation) for conditions on practice, censure or fine, or
any of them together, would be disproportionate to the offending by the
practitioner and would not address the underlying issues of Mr Chum’s
offending in an adequate way. Ultimately the Tribunal concluded it had no
alternative but to order cancellation of Mr Chum’s registration and it also
imposed conditions should Mr Chum ever apply for re-registration. An
order for $40,000 costs was made, being 25% of the total.
b. Derry (143/Phys07/79D), involved a physiotherapist who was found to
have engaged in professional misconduct due to his behaviour towards one
patient. At the completion of a session Mr Derry grabbed the sides of the
patient’s bra by the bra cups and pulled both sides down, exposing her
breasts for about five seconds. Mr Derry was cooperative with the
disciplinary process from the earliest opportunity and admitted that his
conduct amounted to professional misconduct. The Tribunal accepted that
in the period leading up to the incident Mr Derry had been working
excessive hours and had taken steps to address the issues that led to the
offending. They found that there was no evidence of sexual gratification or
stimulation, however a very serious error of judgement had still occurred.
An order for suspension was avoided and conditions were imposed for 12
months including a chaperone requirement with female patients and a
mentoring programme. Mr Derry was censured and ordered to pay a
21

$5000 fine and $5000 in costs.
[54] Added to that of course is Mr Easton’s previous appearance before the Tribunal in June
2023.44
[55] Six counts of professional misconduct were established against him, including those
relating to conduct similar to the conduct before this Tribunal,45 namely that during
appointments with Ms E, Mr Easton hugged Ms E, took off his shirt, failed to provide
appropriate draping and screening, undid her bra without her consent, and did not provide
sufficient information for Ms E to give informed consent. Cumulatively the Tribunal found
that this conduct warranted disciplinary sanction.
[56] It is relevant that his conduct with respect to Ms E occurred in 2019 (after his
treatment of [Mrs S].
[57] With respect to penalty as a result of the 2019 hearing, the Tribunal recognised that Mr
Easton had engaged in the disciplinary process and had accepted responsibility for some
aspects of his conduct. It censured Mr Easton and imposed the following conditions on his
return to practice for two years:
a. Mr Easton is not to practise as a sole practitioner.
b. Mr Easton must practice only in a “Certified practice” audited and
accredited under the Allied Health Sector Standards. It is recommended
that it is of a size that he will not be left to work as a sole provider should
one of the other practitioners be unavailable.
c. Any employer will be provided with a copy of this Tribunal decision.
d. Mr Easton must work under the supervision of a Physiotherapy Board
approved supervisor on the following terms:
i. The supervisor is not from the same practice that employs Mr Easton.
44 (1356/Phys21/519P).
45 The remaining counts related to providing services while suspended, delivering cervical manipulations when
untrained, delivering acupuncture when untrained, and failing to comply with general standards of care
through poor systems and planning.
22

ii. The cost of the supervision is to be met by Mr Easton.
iii. Mr Easton must meet in person with that supervisor at least monthly.
iv. That supervisor is to provide monthly reports to the board on Mr
Easton’s understanding of and compliance with the Board’s
Physiotherapy Standards Framework including:
A. Professionalism
B. Professional development portfolio
C. Informed consent
D. Documentation
E. Clinical reasoning
[58] Alongside these conditions Mr Easton was fined $500. The fine would have been $2000
but was reduced in consideration of Mr Easton’s financial circumstances. He was also
ordered to pay $44,765.47 in costs, being 20% of both the Tribunal and the PCC costs.
[59] Mr Easton advised the Tribunal he did not intend to return to physiotherapy practice.46
He advised the same during this PCC’s investigation and has not sought a practicing
certificate since the 2019 hearing. As such the conditions imposed by the last Tribunal are
still in force.
Aggravating and mitigating factors
[60] The Tribunal accepts that the following are aggravating factors:
a. The charge relates to two discreet occasions: December 2013 and October 2018.
b. Mr Easton’s conduct towards [Mrs S] was not isolated. He has previously been
found to have misconducted himself in a similar way with respect to Ms E.
46 1356/Phys21/519P at [340].
23

c. Mr Easton failed to fulfil core aspects of informed consent which he ought to
have known. He did not describe [Mrs S’] condition to her, he did not describe
the treatment to her, or provide her with the opportunity to ask questions.
Importantly, he did not get her informed consent. This led to [Mrs S] feeling
confused and violated.
d. Mr Easton’s failure to respect [Mrs S’] privacy and dignity by failing to offer and
provide adequate draping/screening left her vulnerable for the totality of the first
appointment. This was not a momentary lapse of judgment. Mr Easton ought to
have been well aware of his professional obligations.
e. Removal of his shirt during physiotherapy treatment demonstrates Mr Easton’s
failure to understand the nature of the professional behaviour expected of
physiotherapists. This failure is exacerbated by the fact that [Mrs S] was naked
from the waist up and not draped when he removed his shirt.
f. Similarly, by hugging [Mrs S], Mr Easton failed to uphold basic professional
boundaries and displayed poor professional judgment. He ought to have
respected [Mrs S] ‘bodily integrity’ by only touching her for clinical reasons.
g. [Mrs S] felt the need to take steps to enforce boundaries between herself and Mr
Easton during the second appointment, including going to another room to
change out of her top and wrapping herself in a towel. [Mrs S’] evidence is that
Mr Easton was angry with her for taking measures to protect her privacy and
dignity. The PCC submits that his conduct is exacerbated by his unprofessional
response to [Mrs S’] actions. In any case, there can be no dispute that the onus
was on him to maintain proper professional boundaries.
h. Mr Easton’s misconduct has caused material harm to [Mrs S]. In relation to her
appointments with Mr Easton, [Mrs S’] evidence is that she felt
“violated”47,“ashamed”48 and “grubby”49 like she had “handed over her
47 [Ms S’] BOE at [19].
48 [Ms S’] BOE at [39].
49 [Ms S’] BOE at [40].
24

autonomy.”50 The harm caused to [Mrs S] reflects the significance of his
misconduct.
[61] To balance the aggravating features it is acknowledged, that while Mr Easton’s conduct
falls within the range of sexually inappropriate behaviour, there is no evidence that he was
sexually motivated.
[62] We have been challenged during this hearing by a lack of engagement by Mr Easton
however it appears to be generally accepted that Mr Easton has not practised since 2019,
suffers from [health condition] and is likely living in straitened circumstances. Mr Easton has
evidently said on multiple occasions that he has no interest in practising physiotherapy again.
Appropriate Penalty
[63] The PCC urged upon us that the only appropriate penalty is one of cancellation. Given
that these charges predate those for which he was before the Tribunal in 2019, we must
consider what additional impact these charges would have had had they been heard at that
time. They are in essence, further examples of some of the offending he was found guilty of
at that time. They in short, add more examples of a person being adversely affected by his
behaviour demonstrating a course of conduct such that the Tribunal is satisfied that nothing
short of cancellation of his registration pursuant to section 101(1) of the Act is an
appropriate penalty and such a cancellation is ordered forthwith.
[64] Pursuant to s 157 of the Act the Tribunal directs the Executive Officer:
(a) To publish this decision and a summary on the Tribunal’s website; and
(b) To request the Physiotherapy Board of New Zealand to publish either a summary
of, or a reference to, the Tribunal’s decision in its professional publications to
members, in either case including a reference to the Tribunal’s website so as to
enable interested parties to access the decision.
50 [Ms S’] BOE at [38]
25

Costs
[65] The PCC urges the Tribunal to make an award of costs. The Tribunal is not persuaded
that such an award should be made for the following reasons:
a. There is no evidence that Mr Easton has the means to meet such an award.
b. There is no evidence that Mr Easton has assets which could be liquidated to
meet such an award.
c. It is understood that Mr Easton paid costs when last before the Tribunal but
this was when he had the benefit of insurance cover. Given as it is
accepted that he has not worked as a physiotherapist since 2019, it is
inconceivable that he has maintained an insurance policy and would have
to rely on his own means for payment.
d. There is no argument that Mr Easton continues to be both [Health
information suppressed by Order of Tribunal] and thought to be
unemployed.
[66] In these circumstances, no order for costs is made.
Orders for Suppression
[67] On the 11th of September 2025, the Tribunal made an order permanently suppressing
the name and any identifying details of [Mrs S] pursuant s 95 (2)(d) of the Act.
[68] Mr Easton’s name was published as a result of the 2019 proceedings. He has not made
an application for suppression, and no order is made in respect of him. However, details of
his [health] are suppressed.
DATED at New Plymouth this 16th day of December 2025
S Hughes KC
Deputy Chair
Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal
